title: Wild Sharks Hear Sounds From 243 Feet Away and Know Which Direction They Came From
summary:
The ocean is full of sound, and for sharks, those sounds carry information about what's happening far beyond their view. Noise from prey, predators, and other animals may reveal what's going on in the surrounding water. But until now, scientists had little direct evidence of how far a free-swimming shark can hear — or whether it can tell where a sound came from.

A new study from Florida Atlantic University used an underwater speaker, a drone, and wild blacktip sharks off Florida's coast. The sharks detected low-frequency sounds from up to 74 meters (243 feet) away — farther than any previous demonstration in freely swimming sharks. Even more striking: they often made rapid turns away from the speaker, proving they could pinpoint the sound's direction. The findings were published in Integrative Organismal Biology.

Blacktips were a good choice because large numbers gather along the Palm Beach County coast each winter, and the clear, shallow water let researchers watch individual sharks from above. "Their abundance and accessibility made it possible for us to observe them from above without disturbing their natural behavior, while also presenting controlled underwater sounds," says senior author Stephen Kajiura.

"What makes this finding particularly interesting is that the sharks were responding to sounds beyond the acoustic near field," Kajiura says. "This suggests they are detecting the particle motion associated with sound even at considerable distances."

The team played three ranges of low-frequency sounds (100–800 Hertz) and a 10 kiloHertz control sound beyond sharks' hearing range. The sharks reacted to all three low ranges but ignored the control. A drone flying 40–50 meters above recorded their movements, which researchers analyzed frame by frame.

Sharks lack the gas-filled swim bladder that helps bony fish detect sound pressure. Instead, they rely on their inner ears, including a structure called the macula neglecta, which may detect vibrations as sound travels through water.

The study also shows why ocean experiments matter. In a tank, sound bounces off walls, creating confusing signals. "It is like being in a house of mirrors," says lead author Caroline Sullivan. In the open ocean, wild sharks gave natural responses.

Understanding shark hearing could help scientists protect these predators — and better understand how they navigate their noisy underwater world.
why_it_matters: The ocean is getting louder — shipping, sonar and underwater construction all add sound — so knowing how far sharks can hear, and how precisely they can locate a source, is a first step toward understanding whether human noise is changing where these top predators hunt, feed and travel.

They stopped moving completely

background_read: Sharks are cartilaginous fish — their skeletons are made of flexible cartilage instead of bone — and their group has been swimming in the oceans since long before the dinosaurs. Unlike bony fish, they have no gas-filled swim bladder, so they cannot detect sound the way a goldfish does; instead they appear to pick up the tiny vibrations created as a sound wave passes through water. Sharks also read their world with a lateral line (a row of pressure-sensitive cells along their bodies) and with special organs that detect the weak electric fields given off by living animals.

Sound behaves very differently underwater than in air: it travels roughly four and a half times faster and can carry for kilometres, which is why biologists sometimes describe the ocean as a 'soundscape' rather than a landscape. Marine biologists have studied shark hearing for decades, but almost always with captive animals in tanks, where echoes from the walls distort the results. Florida Atlantic University (a research university in Boca Raton, Florida, known for its marine science programmes) runs long-term studies of the blacktip sharks that migrate along Florida's Atlantic coast each winter, and its team used a drone to watch wild sharks from above. The findings were published in Integrative Organismal Biology, a journal that covers how animals function.

perspectives.description: This is the first clean evidence from wild, free-swimming sharks, and it suggests their hearing is better than lab studies implied. It also validates a method — drone plus underwater speaker — that can be reused on other species without capturing them.

The result covers one species, in one place, tested with a few low-frequency sounds. Turning away could mean fleeing rather than 'locating' a source, and small samples and wild conditions always leave room for doubt.

Fish hearing was long studied in tanks simply because tanks are convenient, and the echoes made the results hard to trust. This work belongs to a wider shift toward field experiments with drones and remote sensors that leave animal behaviour untouched.

Testing other shark species and higher frequencies, and measuring how much ship and construction noise actually reaches them, could turn this finding into practical tools such as acoustic deterrents that keep sharks away from fishing nets and beaches.
